items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I had Herman Chittison on piano and Eugene d'Hellemes on bass. I believe it was the first jazz trip in the history of recording to be composed of trumpet, piano and bass.

ctx.x: Another musician and song writer that I had seen in New York who was now living in Paris was Spencer Williams who composed the famous "Basin Street Blues". I met the members of Willy Lewis's band that were not with him when I met him in the south of France. Joe Hayman played alto-sax and Frank "Big-Boy" Goodie, tenor and clarinet, who was really a big boy about 7 feet tall and must have weighed 280 pounds. He had also played cornet but eventually gave it up. Johnny Mitchell was the guitarist.

I think that Garnet had worked a short while with Willy and it did not go so well because Garnet was quite wild and flighty. So Willy had engaged Herman Chittison whom I had met some years before in Boston accompanying the comedian Stepan Fetchet.

One week after I had started playing at the Villa d'Este I was able to go from Place Pigalle to the Etoile or Arc de Triomphe with the bus and I had the feeling that I was learning more about the great city of Paris. items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I had Herman Chittison on piano... We recorded 'What's The Reason' and 'Georgia on my Mind'.

ctx.x: January 24th 1936, I recorded for the first time under my own name. The date was supervised by Hughes Penassie and I had Herman Chittison on piano and Eugene d'Hellemes on bass. I believe it was the first jazz trip in the history of recording to be composed of trumpet, piano and bass. We recorded "What's The Reason" and "Georgia on my Mind". I had only heard Chittison play one time and that was when I first met him in 1932

in Boston. "Chit" was fast as [and] lightning and he must have heard Art Tatum many times and studied his style. He was the next thing to Art as far as technique was concerned. But he never wanted to bass to accompany him on his solos. He had a good left hand and I suppose he had the idea that the bass did not play the same pattern as he did with his left hand and it disturbed his ideas.

D'Hellemes was a good solid bass player who preferred to play trombone. He was also a very agreable fellow and we began to be good friends although I did not speak French and he didn't speak English. The first date with Chit and Eugene was recorded for Ultraphone. We recorded again the 31st of January '36 for His Master's Voice and did "I'm in the Mood for Love" and "After You've Gone".
